lesson.title: One Molecule, One Crystal, Trillions of Bonds
lesson.summary: Network covalent solids are extended structures in which every atom is linked to its neighbors by covalent bonds throughout the entire crystal, making the whole solid behave essentially as one giant molecule.
lesson.body:
Most covalent compounds exist as discrete, individual molecules, small clusters of atoms like CO2 or H2O that are held together internally by strong covalent bonds but only weakly attracted to their neighbors. Network covalent solids break that pattern entirely. Instead of covalent bonds being confined inside small molecular units, they extend continuously through the whole sample, so that a crystal of a network covalent solid is, strictly speaking, a single enormous molecule containing an essentially unlimited number of atoms all connected by the same kind of covalent bonds already introduced. Understanding this structure requires combining two ideas directly: the strong, directional, electron sharing nature of covalent bonds, and the ordered, repeating three dimensional arrangement described by a crystal lattice.

Diamond is the clearest example. Each carbon atom in diamond forms four covalent bonds to four neighboring carbon atoms arranged tetrahedrally, and each of those neighbors is likewise bonded to four more carbons, and so on throughout the entire crystal. There is no natural boundary marking off one molecule from the next, because the bonding network simply keeps going in every direction. This is fundamentally different from a molecular solid like ice, where individual H2O molecules sit in a lattice held together by comparatively weak intermolecular attractions between distinct molecules; in diamond, there are no separate molecules to attract each other in the first place, only one continuous bonded structure.

Quartz, silicon dioxide, is another important example, built from a repeating network in which each silicon atom is covalently bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen bridges two silicon atoms, again extending throughout the crystal with no discrete molecular units. Graphite offers a more nuanced case worth noting: within each layer, carbon atoms are covalently bonded to three neighbors in a continuous two dimensional sheet, making that layer a network covalent structure in two dimensions, but the layers themselves are stacked and held together only by weak intermolecular forces, which is why graphite sheets slide past each other easily even though breaking a bond within a layer is very difficult.

The properties of network covalent solids follow directly from having covalent bonds, rather than weaker intermolecular attractions, running through the entire structure. Melting or breaking a network covalent solid means breaking a large number of strong covalent bonds throughout the lattice, not just overcoming weak attractions between separate molecules, so these solids typically have extremely high melting points, diamond melts only above 3500 degrees Celsius under normal pressure, and are extremely hard, since deforming the structure also requires breaking covalent bonds. They are usually poor electrical conductors as well, since diamond and quartz have no freely moving charge carriers, though graphite is a notable exception because of delocalized electrons within its bonded sheets. This combination of extreme hardness, very high melting point, and often low conductivity is the practical signature chemists use to recognize a network covalent solid from its physical properties alone.
